history.heading: Shipwreck and settlement
paragraphs: Bermuda, a small group of islands in the North Atlantic about 1,000 km off the coast of North Carolina, was uninhabited when the Spanish navigator Juan de Bermúdez sighted it in the early 16th century. Its reefs gave it a reputation as the "Isle of Devils".

In 1609 the English ship Sea Venture, bound for Virginia, was wrecked there, an event that may have inspired Shakespeare's The Tempest. Permanent settlement began in 1612, and St. George's, founded that year, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited English towns in the Americas and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.heading: Colony and naval base
paragraphs: Bermuda's economy relied on shipbuilding, salt trading and seafaring, using enslaved Africans and Native Americans; slavery was abolished in 1834. Britain built a major naval dockyard on the islands, and the United States had military bases there during and after the Second World War.
Racial segregation persisted into the 1960s. Voters rejected independence from Britain in a 1995 referendum.

culture.heading: Island traditions
paragraphs: Bermudian culture blends British, African, Caribbean and Portuguese (Azorean) influences. Gombey dancers, with masks and drums, perform at festivals. Cup Match, a two-day cricket match and public holiday that commemorates emancipation, is the biggest event of the year.
Bermuda gave its name to Bermuda shorts, worn with knee socks as business attire. Fish chowder with sherry pepper and rum is a signature dish, and the Dark 'n' Stormy cocktail originated there.

politics.heading: Self-governing territory
paragraphs: Bermuda is the oldest British Overseas Territory and is largely self-governing. Its Parliament, first convened in 1620, is one of the oldest in the world. A premier leads the government, while a governor appointed by the British monarch handles defence, foreign affairs and internal security.

economy.heading: Insurance and finance
paragraphs: Bermuda is one of the world's wealthiest places per person. International business, especially insurance and reinsurance, is the dominant industry, attracted by the absence of corporate income tax and strong regulation; Bermuda introduced a corporate tax for large multinationals in 2025 in line with global rules.
Tourism, centred on pink-sand beaches and golf, is the second pillar. The Bermudian dollar is pegged to the US dollar, and living costs are among the highest in the world.
